links.outcome: Readability (FRES, FKGL) of AI answers to shoulder arthroplasty patient questions
links.effect: ChatGPT majority of FRES scores <20 (academic-level text); CoPilot FRES >30 but still required minimum 12th-grade education; CoPilot easier to read (P = .0031).
links.quote: Although answers provided by CoPilot were "easier" to read, they still required a 12th-grade education, which may be too complex for most patients, posing a challenge for patient comprehension.

links.outcome: Reading level of AI-generated patient information versus appropriate patient reading level
links.effect: ChatGPT FRES mostly <20 with academic-level FKGL; CoPilot required at least 12th-grade education, likely too complex for most patients.
links.quote: In comparison, the ChatGPT generated more complex texts, with the majority of the FRES scores <20, and FKGL score signifying complexity of academic level text.

links.outcome: Quality and source types of citations provided by CoPilot
links.effect: CoPilot provided citations; academic sources 31.1% (rTSA) and 26.7% (aTSA); substantial nonmedical media and commercial sources cited. ChatGPT gave no citations (JAMA score 0 vs 3).
links.quote: There were a substantial amount of nonmedical media sites, and commercial sources that were cited for both aTSA and rTSA questions by CoPilot.

screen.reason: Evaluates and compares the quality, readability, and accuracy of patient-facing information generated by ChatGPT-3.5 and Microsoft Copilot regarding shoulder arthroplasty without testing a specific organizational safeguard or deployment intervention.
